title: Building Susinsight's AI Research Assistant
description: Designing and shipping an AI research assistant for Susinsight that answers sustainability questions using only its own published content, and the lessons learned along the way.
content:
The Susinsight team wanted a way for readers to ask questions and get answers drawn from their own reporting, not from the general internet. The goal was straightforward: someone should be able to ask "how are carbon credit schemes affecting smallholder farmers in Kenya?" and get a response grounded in Susinsight's own coverage of that topic, with sources and links to the original stories.

I led the design and implementation of this feature over the course of a few months. Here's what we built, how it works, and some of the lessons that shaped it.

What we built

The AI Research Assistant (called Ask Susinsight) lives in two places: a dedicated /ask page and a floating modal that follows readers around the site. Both use the same backend: type a question, get a paragraph answer with numbered sources. It's designed to feel like asking a knowledgeable editor rather than chatting with a chatbot.

Suggested image: A screenshot of the Ask Susinsight interface showing a question, answer, and source cards side by side. This gives visitors an immediate visual sense of what the feature looks and feels like.

How it works (the simple version)

At its core, the system uses a technique called Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG for short. Here's what that actually means in practice:

Step one: indexing. Every Susinsight article is split into chunks of text, and each chunk is converted into a numerical representation called an embedding (think of it as a fingerprint that captures the chunk's meaning). These embeddings are stored in a vector database, a specialised database designed to search by similarity rather than by exact keywords.

Step two: retrieval. When a reader asks a question, the system converts that question into an embedding too. Then it searches the vector database for article chunks whose fingerprints are most similar to the question's fingerprint. The top matches, usually four to six chunks from different articles, are collected.

Step three: generation. Those matched chunks are stitched into a prompt that tells an LLM (a large language model, the technology behind tools like ChatGPT) to answer the question using only the provided text. The LLM writes a flowing paragraph answer, and the system appends links to the actual articles as sources.

Suggested image: A simple flowchart showing this pipeline: Question, Convert to embedding, Search vector database, Retrieve article chunks, Build prompt, LLM, Answer with sources. This helps readers who are less familiar with AI understand the architecture at a glance without needing to read through the entire explanation.

The tech stack

The system runs on several services, each chosen for a specific reason:

Upstash Vector stores the article embeddings. It's serverless, so there's no database server to manage, and it scales to zero when nobody is using it. This keeps costs predictable for a platform that doesn't yet have millions of queries.

Jina AI generates the embeddings. Their model (jina-embeddings-v2-base-en) converts text into those numerical fingerprints. I chose it because it handles mixed-length content well, a Susinsight article could be a short news brief or a long-form investigation.

Groq serves the LLM. The model running behind the scenes is LLaMA 3.1 8B, a lightweight but capable open-weight model that runs fast enough to return answers in under two seconds. Groq's custom hardware makes inference unusually quick for this class of model.

Upstash Redis handles rate limiting, a simple counter per IP address that resets every hour, keeping the free tier safe from abuse.

Next.js is the application framework, deployed via Cloudflare. The server actions that handle questions run as API endpoints, while the UI components (the modal, the /ask page, the floating button) are React client components rendered in the browser.

Early challenges and how we fixed them

A few things went wrong in the first version. Each one taught us something about how to make AI assistants that are genuinely useful rather than just technically impressive.

Challenge 1: The assistant kept inventing article titles. When the LLM couldn't find a good source for a claim, it would make one up, a completely fabricated headline that sounded plausible. This is a well-known risk with LLMs. We solved it by moving the "related reading" section out of the LLM's hands entirely. The app now picks those additional articles in code using the same vector search scores, so readers only ever see titles that come from real published content.

Challenge 2: The answers felt hollow. Someone asked "Is there a link between culture and sustainability in Africa?" and got an answer that name-dropped a steel decarbonisation project as a cultural example. The article itself said nothing about culture, the LLM had just retroactively labelled it as one because it mentioned sustainability. This forced us to add stricter rules to the prompt: define the concept first (what does "culture" mean in this context?), show the mechanism (what specific practice or belief affects what outcome?), and don't use an article as an example unless the article genuinely demonstrates the connection. We also expanded the search query to include related terms: when someone asks about "culture", the system now also searches for traditions, beliefs, customs, heritage, language, and ritual behind the scenes, which surfaces the right articles in the first place.

Challenge 3: The search returned irrelevant articles. A question about culture would pull up articles about infrastructure or finance because those articles happened to mention "sustainability in Africa" somewhere. The solution was two-fold: we added each article's section tag (for example, "Cultural Stories" vs "Business Stories") into the context so the LLM could judge relevance for itself, and we added query expansion: if the question mentions certain keywords, related terms are appended to the search before embedding, which pulls in better matches from the vector database.

Challenge 4: Rate limiting. With an API-powered assistant, one aggressive user could rack up significant costs. We implemented a simple rate limit of 10 questions per hour per IP address using Redis. The user sees how many questions they have left only when they drop below 3, to keep the interface clean.

What's next

The assistant works well for its current scope, but there's a clear direction for improvement. The quality of answers still depends heavily on what's in the vector database: if Susinsight hasn't published an article that directly addresses a topic, the system will describe the closest coverage it has rather than refusing to answer, but the result is inevitably thinner. Expanding the content base with more articles and possibly indexing select external sources (like the Substack newsletter) would broaden the assistant's range.

The prompt engineering is also iterative. Each conversation with the editorial team reveals new edge cases where the model misinterprets what it has. I expect the prompt rules to keep evolving as we see more real-world questions and the team's expectations sharpen.

There's also the question of how readers discover the assistant. Right now it's surfaced through a floating button on the site, a link in the main navigation, and a sidebar card on story pages. Each of these was designed to feel native to the Susinsight experience rather than like an inserted chatbot widget. We'll likely add more entry points as usage grows, a /ask link in article footers, for instance, or inline question prompts within story pages based on the topic being read.

A few readers have asked whether the assistant could eventually answer questions with data from Susdata (Susinsight's data initiative section), combining narrative articles with structured data like indicators and metrics. That's a harder technical problem because it means merging vector search with structured querying, but it's the most promising direction for making the assistant genuinely useful for researchers and policymakers, not just casual readers.

What it taught me

RAG systems are deceptively simple in theory and surprisingly subtle in practice. The pipeline is three steps, but each step hides decisions that determine whether the system feels intelligent or clueless.

The largest lesson: prompt engineering is not about clever tricks. It's about being precise about what you want and honest about what the model cannot do. Every rule we added came from a real failure that a reader or editor noticed. The assistant is better not because the prompt is longer, but because it encodes the hard-earned constraints of the editorial team's standards.

The second lesson: retrieval quality matters more than the LLM. A perfect model fed the wrong articles will still give bad answers. Investing in better search (query expansion, metadata tagging, score thresholds) produced bigger improvements than swapping the model would have.

The third lesson: rate limits, error states, and degraded experiences are not afterthoughts. The assistant is most fragile when something fails, the embedding API goes down, the vector query times out, or the rate limit kicks in. Each of those moments needs a deliberate response that protects the user's trust, not just the system's cost.
